units.text: You’ll learn to tell block storage, a shared Linux file system, and a specialized managed file system apart. E B S is a persistent block device for E C two. The operating system treats it as a disk, so it can hold a boot file system or database data. In the same Availability Zone, the disk can retain its data when detached and attached again. Choose capacity, I ops, and throughput for the workload.

To recover in another zone, take a snapshot and create a new volume there. You do not move the original volume between zones. E B S is not a shared NFS or SMB file system; supported Multi-Attach configurations are a specialized block-storage exception.

Choose EFS when several Linux applications need to see the same files. The clients reach mount targets through NFS. The targets in the two zones lead to one Regional file system and the same POSIX directory tree. If one client writes a report, another authorized client can read it from that tree.
Regional EFS stores data across Availability Zones; One Zone does not. Clients still need network connectivity and the correct file permissions. This is managed NFS, not a native Windows SMB share.

Choose FSx by the client's protocol and the work it must do. A Windows team share needs SMB, directory identity and Windows permissions. Lustre suits parallel HPC or machine-learning workers sharing a working file system.

ONTAP meets supported combinations of file and block needs, such as NFS, SMB and iSCSI. OpenZFS fits NFS workloads that benefit from ZFS snapshots and clones. A W S operates the file-system infrastructure, but protocol, performance and recovery requirements still decide which family fits.

You’ll learn to match a database to your workload and check what an RDS client needs to connect. Start from the application's question, not the database label. For joining orders and customers and committing a payment, start with relational SQL such as RDS or Aurora. When the common request is fetching an order by known key, DynamoDB can fit a deliberately designed key access pattern.

Use a time-series engine for sensor trends, and a document database for nested document access. OpenSearch fits relevance-ranked product search. ElastiCache answers repeated hot reads fast, but is not the authoritative order store here. Check consistency, capacity, and recovery goals before deciding.

Follow a SQL client through a DNS endpoint and engine port, then a security group, to the managed DB instance. The instance combines an engine and version, compute class, storage, and database settings such as a parameter group. Those are independent choices: a larger disk does not automatically tune a query.

The DB subnet group supplies eligible subnets, ordinarily across at least two Availability Zones. A Single-AZ DB instance still occupies one zone at a time. Multi-AZ is a separate availability choice. Standard RDS does not give you host login access, and SQL grants remain database permissions.

RDS takes on provisioning and platform jobs, including eligible patching, automated backups, and monitoring. The application owner still designs the schema and indexes, tunes queries, manages database roles, and chooses capacity. Start by checking that the available engine and version support what the application needs.

In this example, the hundred-gibibyte volume can grow within the configured autoscaling maximum. It does not shrink automatically. If the queueing comes from connection pressure, CPU, or a slow query plan, growing storage is not the diagnosis.

Trace the orders function over private DNS and routing to the database endpoint, then through a security-group rule for its engine port. A role does not create a network route, and an open port does not give SQL permission. TLS protects the session in transit.

In the PostgreSQL example, the function connects on port fifty-four thirty-two, authenticates as the application reader, and needs a separate SELECT grant to retrieve the order row. If nothing connects, check the route and port first. If the user connects but SELECT fails, inspect the database grants.

You’ll learn to separate recovery history, failover, and read scaling, then route replicas for the right purpose. Backups answer which earlier state you can recover. Automated backups and transaction logs enable point-in-time restore within the retention window to a new database resource. Validate the data, permissions, and replacement endpoint before cutting the application over.

Use a manual snapshot when you want a deliberate recovery point retained until deletion. A supported cross-account or cross-Region copy also needs the right encryption and key permissions. A live replica serves traffic; it does not give you a retained history of prior data.

For classic RDS Multi-AZ DB instance availability, the primary writer synchronously replicates to a standby. The standby does not serve read traffic. On failover the application reconnects through its DB endpoint; test that your client handles the interruption.

For offloading reads, use eligible read replicas and send read traffic to their endpoints. They copy asynchronously and can lag, so use the writer when a workflow must see a just-committed change. Cross-Region replicas are supported in applicable configurations, but are not backup history.

A Multi-AZ DB cluster is not the classic one-standby deployment. The classic standby is not readable. The cluster shown places one writer and two readable instances across three zones; replication is semisynchronous. Use the writer endpoint for writes and the reader endpoint for suitable read connections.
The exam cue is whether the requirement includes read capacity as well as availability. Verify engine support, cost, and how the application reconnects before selecting the more capable deployment.

Weighted Route Fifty-Three DNS chooses answers to fresh lookups. Giving reader A weight eighty and reader B twenty does not mean eighty percent of SQL queries go to A. The application makes database connections after DNS resolution.

Cached answers can steer new connections until their time to live expires; open pooled connections are not moved. Keep writes on the primary and compare connections, query load, and lag on the readers. Those measurements reveal the actual split.

You’ll learn where RDS encryption and auditing apply, and what an I A M database login token actually authorizes. Protect each layer separately. K M S encryption protects stored RDS data and snapshots when configured. TLS with certificate verification protects in-transit connections. CloudTrail records service API activity, not the text of a SQL statement. Use supported engine audit or query logs for that investigation.

Engine features such as Oracle or SQL Server TDE are separate where supported. To migrate an unencrypted RDS instance to encryption, take a snapshot, make an encrypted copy, then restore a new encrypted resource and validate the application before switching.

For supported RDS engines, I A M database authentication gives a signed login token for the database endpoint, port and matching user. Prepare the I A M principal with database-connect permission and the corresponding database user. Use TLS to connect.

The token has a fifteen-minute login window, not a fifteen-minute SQL session limit. The established session continues after token expiry. The login identifies the user; SQL grants separately decide whether that user can SELECT.

You’ll learn to choose a supported Oracle recovery path and verify a controlled MySQL cutover. Decide where Oracle must run after recovery. For the managed RDS path, restore the RDS snapshot or automated backup into a new RDS DB instance, then validate that the application connects and uses the intended data.

For a supported self-managed Oracle target, the diagram uses the RDS administrative RMAN package, stages eligible backup files through S three, and restores on the self-managed host. Check versions, backup compatibility, and TDE requirements first. Standard RDS does not supply host or SYS access or Oracle RAC.

Seed the compatible MySQL target from a consistent export, then use supported binary-log or GTID replication to catch up. Keep writes on the source during catch-up. For cutover, pause writes, verify sync and replication errors, validate the target, and switch the application only once it is ready.

If no target writes occurred, you can route back to the validated source and resume writes there. After the target accepted writes, the old source alone is stale. Pause and reconcile those writes with tested reverse replication or a recovery plan before switching back.
